AVL Panelling Convergence Study

How coarse can the vortex-lattice mesh be for a blended-wing-body design sweep before the numbers stop deciding the aircraft correctly? A pre-registered, gated study across eight stages.

Result · escalate

No affordable mesh passes all seven gates.

The study's own rule (§7) forbids inventing a winner by relaxing a threshold. The ranking of designs is rock-solid at every mesh tested — Spearman ≥ 0.99, zero objective regret, zero trim/stability label flips. What the cheap meshes cannot yet resolve is absolute elevon effectiveness: the control-surface power and the trim deflections that flow from it. Two gates bind — gate 4 (coefficient uncertainty < 1%) and gate 6 (trim deflection error ≤ 0.5°).

The concrete stake, measured honestly in Stage 7: a 2000-design × 3-angle sweep costs ~140 h at the production mesh versus ~19 h at the cheapest ranking-safe mesh — a 7.3× wall-clock difference. The three defensible paths:

c16s2u · 19 h

Screening / ranking. Ranking is provably intact (ρ 0.996, 0% regret, 0 label flips) and this holds regardless of control state (Stage 6b). The pragmatic choice for a large sweep whose job is to rank designs — 7.3× faster than production.

c24s4c · 140 h

Least-bad for absolute numbers. The finest affordable mesh, but it does not clear gate 4: measured directly, worst-case coefficient error is ~3% (not the 0.8% the planning model predicted). Use only knowing it is ~1.5–3% optimistic on drag / elevon power.

escalate

If <1% on absolute effectiveness is required. No affordable AVL mesh delivers it — every tested mesh fails gate 4 by 2–36×. The vortex-lattice + strip-viscous model is at its resolution limit for control-surface loading; a higher-fidelity hinge treatment is the real fix.

Recommendation — for ranking-driven screening (what a 2000-design sweep usually is), use c16s2u at 19 h; Stages 6 and 6b prove the ranking is untouched. For any run feeding absolute drag / control-authority numbers downstream, there is no clean mesh — even production carries ~3% worst-case error — so escalate the model. Nothing is recorded as "passing"; the gates say escalate, and that stands. Gate 4 in this report is the audited, directly-measured value (see §Validation), not the original interpolated estimate.

Setup & method

The question is deceptively practical: an optimiser will call AVL thousands of times over a blended-wing-body (BWB) design space, and the panelling density sets both the cost per call and the trustworthiness of every number it returns. Too fine and the sweep is unaffordable; too coarse and the optimiser chases mesh artefacts instead of aerodynamics. This study finds the coarsest mesh that still gets the decisions right — not merely the coefficients.

SolverVortex lattice with per-strip viscous correction

AVL (Athena Vortex Lattice) is driven as a subprocess through the MACH-Aero / pyGeo stack. The wing is discretised into a lattice of horseshoe vortices — chordwise panels along the flow, spanwise strips across it. Each spanwise strip additionally receives a NeuralFoil viscous profile-drag correction, so cd_total and l_over_d carry a real boundary-layer term, not just induced drag. AVL's influence matrix is independent of angle of attack — only the right-hand side changes with α — which is why mesh sensitivity is expected to be weakly angle-dependent and why a handful of angles suffices.

The runbook originally listed +8° for the convergence stages. Stage 0 resolved the inconsistency against workflow.py: production does not sweep +8°, so it was removed from Stages 2–3 rather than added to Stage 6 (decision D2).

Control stateWhy validate at a differential deflection?

Production flies a symmetric-only elevon sweep {−5, 0, +5}° with zero differential. The study deliberately validates the mesh at (sym +4, diff +4) instead. Antisymmetric loading carries a higher spanwise wavenumber than symmetric loading, so a mesh proven adequate under differential deflection is conservative for the symmetric case it will actually run (decision D1). Stage 6b closes the loop by re-testing at zero deflection and confirming the transfer holds.

Derived in Stage 6 — no extra runs: delta_trim = −cm / elevon_sym.Cm (units: per-degree, asserted in Stage 0 — getting this wrong silently scales every trim by 57.3), static_margin = (x_np − x_ref)/mac, and roll_power = elevon_diff.Cl. Hinge moments are in the list because they size the servos and, being hinge-line quantities, are the most panel-sensitive things the model produces.

Two methodological floors that govern every stage

Print-noise floor (§4.5, 1e−4). AVL prints six decimals, i.e. ~1e−6 resolution. A relative error taken against a near-zero comparator (the lateral derivatives Cnb, elevon_diff.Cn/CY, and the hinge moments) is a ratio of rounding artefacts. Any quantity whose main-effect signal falls below 1e−4 is marked mesh-insensitive and assessed on a normalised discrepancy instead of a meaningless percentage. Richardson / GCI. Where a quantity is monotone and in its asymptotic range, the finest mesh carries a Grid Convergence Index (safety factor Fs = 1.25, refinement ratio r = 2); where it is not, only a finest-grid discrepancy is reported and no convergence is claimed — an honest bound, not an unearned one.

The mesh, and the strip-count correction

Three knobs set the lattice: chordwise panel count (streamwise resolution — captures the pressure recovery and control-surface loading), spanwise strip multiplier (lateral resolution — captures the loading distribution and, through the per-strip viscous term, profile drag), and spacing — how panels are distributed, from uniform (cspace 0.0) to full cosine clustering at the edges (cspace 1.0).

Surprise found in Stage 0 — the runbook under-counted strips

The runbook assumed the 25 defined sections survive into 48 strips at span 2. But snap_sections_to_control=true inserts ~4 sections at the elevon edges, so the realised section count is N = 28–29 and the true strip count is 2 · (N−1) · spanwise — 56 base strips, not 48. This made exactly one planned cell illegal (Stage 1's chord-20 × span-6 = 6720 vortices > 6000 cap); it was capped to chord 16 (decision D4). Every legality check downstream uses the corrected formula.

Vortex count — the real cost driver — is chordwise × strips. Two very different meshes can therefore cost the same: the production c24s4c (24×216 ≈ 5376 vortices) and the comparator c48s2c (48×108 ≈ 5376) land on the same ~84 s, a fact that becomes decisive in Stage 7.

1

Separability of the two lattice axes

108 runs · chord{8,12,16} × span{2,4,6} × 4 geoms × angles{−2,0,4} · 0 failures

The whole strategy of tuning chordwise and spanwise resolution separately (Stages 2 and 3) is only valid if the two axes do not interact. Stage 1 tests that directly with a two-way, no-replication ANOVA decomposition on every quantity: split each 3×3 table into a chord main-effect A, a span main-effect B, and an interaction residual AB, then form the interaction index I = rms(AB) / (rms(A)+rms(B)). Small I means the axes are separable.

Why the noise floor matters here

A naïve pass flagged Cnb at I = 0.53 and looked like a failure. But raw Cnb moved 0.001536→0.001543 — seven counts in the last printed digit, pure rounding, not interaction. Applying the pre-committed §4.5 floor, mesh-insensitive quantities (Cnb, the elevon_diff lateral terms, both hinge moments) are set aside from the ratio test and assessed on normalised interaction (all < 0.5%). This is executing a rule fixed in advance, not tuning to pass.

Chordwise convergence

128 runs · chord{6,12,24,48} · 32 (geom × angle) cells · chain B = 12→24→48 · 0 failures

This is the dominant axis of the error budget. Four chordwise densities are run so that two overlapping ratio-2 Richardson chains (6→12→24 and 12→24→48) can be formed; agreement between the chains is itself a test of asymptotic behaviour. The "knee" is where adding chordwise panels stops buying accuracy.

Design implication

Spanwise resolution is cheap accuracy that is nearly spent by span 2. There is no reason to pay for span 4 unless a quantity specifically demands it — which is why the production default's span 4 looks like over-resolution of the axis that matters least.

Panel spacing — cosine vs uniform

48 main + 4 comparator + 4 reference-neutrality runs · α +4 only · 0 failures

Does clustering panels toward the edges (cosine) beat spreading them evenly (uniform)? First a reference-neutrality check: at chord 48 the two spacings agree to within 0.23% worst-case, confirming the comparator itself is spacing-independent and can serve as a fair reference. Then the sweep — and the answer is unambiguous.

Ranking & decision test — the decisive stage

540 runs · 30 normal + 6 extreme geoms · angles{−2,0,4} · seven gates · 100% success

Everything prior is preparation; this is the test. A cheap mesh is acceptable only if it preserves the decisions an optimiser would make — the design ranking, the top-10 set, the trim and stability classifications — not merely the coefficients. Seven gates test that directly on the 30 normal designs. The six extremes are reported separately (a failure there is a documented limitation, not a disqualification).

Gate 4Coefficient uncertainty < 1% — measured directly, none pass

No mesh clears gate 4. Measured directly from the 30-design Stage-6 solves, worst-case coefficient error at +4° is c8s2u 6.96%, c12s2u 3.19%, c16s2u 2.22%, c24s4c 2.95% — all far above 1%. (The original report scored gate 4 from a Stage-5 interpolated model that read 0.79% for production; that model was ~3× optimistic. The correction is documented in §Validation and does not change the escalate verdict — it strengthens it.) The error is concentrated in the deflected-elevon camber loading, exactly where chordwise resolution is weakest (Stage 2), and is worse still at α 0.

Gate 5Control-derivative bias & scatter

All five control derivatives keep their sign at every mesh, and the gated pair (elevon_sym.Cm, elevon_diff.Cl) hold |bias| ≤ 5% and scatter ≤ 5% of bias — gate 5 passes for all. (A first pass mis-computed scatter as a fraction of |bias−1|, dividing by near-zero for well-converged settings; corrected to a fraction of the mean ratio, all pass.) The systematic under-prediction is unmistakable — bias is negative and shrinks monotonically as the mesh refines:

Selection rule outcome (§7)

Nothing passes all seven gates. Per the rule, no gate is lowered and no winner is invented: the design tier needs a more expensive discretisation than hoped. The ranking is robust; the elevon effectiveness is under-resolved at every affordable mesh.

Caveats carried on the record

The "trimmable" label uses a documented ±25° envelope. Extreme geometries are not pooled into these statistics. The comparator (chord 48/span 2) is itself ~1.5% short on elevon power per Stage 2 — it is the best available reference, not ground truth, so even c24s4c's 0.79% is measured against an optimistic yardstick.

Deflection sensitivity — does the control state matter?

120 runs · 5 settings × 8 geoms × angles{−2,0,4} · all at zero deflection

The mesh was validated at (sym+4, diff+4) but production flies diff = 0. Decision D1 argued the differential state is conservative; Stage 6b tests that transfer by re-running the convergence subset at zero deflection and comparing the ranking statistics. (A hash-level check first confirms the cache genuinely distinguishes the two control states — a (0,0) cell and its (+4,+4) twin hash apart, so these are real solves, not cache collisions.)

The high-sweep planform dominates the extreme error: 15.2% at c8, falling monotonically to under 1% at the production mesh — the most oblique flow is where a coarse chordwise lattice struggles most. Yet even on the worst extreme, all five control-derivative signs are preserved at every mesh, so no cheap setting would invert a control response. The extremes reinforce, rather than change, the Stage-6 conclusion: the shortfall is elevon/chordwise resolution, and it closes with chordwise count.

7

Honest timings

25 runs · 5 settings × 5 repeats · strictly serial · cache bypassed · alone on a quiet machine

A timing taken while other jobs share the machine is not a timing; a timing from cache is not a timing. Stage 7 re-measures each setting five times, serially, with the cache bypassed, so the cost feeding the selection rule is real end-to-end wall-clock — including the ~1.4 s fixed per-design section build.

The sharp finding

The production mesh costs the same as the comparator — ~84 s each — because both sit near the vortex cap (~5376 vortices). "Production" buys no speed over the reference it approximates. The only setting that is both genuinely cheap and near-passing on gate 6 is c16s2u at 19 h — a 7.3× saving over the 140 h production mesh. That ratio is the entire economic stake behind the gate-4/gate-6 discussion.

The seven gates, in full

7Run success rate100%all pass

Gate 1 carries a displacement clause because global Spearman alone permits one design sliding nine ranks while everything else stays put — the precise failure the study exists to prevent. Gate 2 is reported but noted as uninformative here: the rank-10/11 gap (~1.45%) is comparable to the settings' own uncertainty, so the study rests on gates 3, 4 and 6. Gates 5 and 6 exist because a uniform 30% error in elevon power preserves every ranking yet shifts every trim deflection by 30%, moving designs across the feasibility boundary — gate 6 tests that decision directly.

Validation & audit

The study's gates were re-derived independently from the raw per-run data (all_runs.csv) to check that the code implements the spec. Six of the seven gates reproduce exactly; one did not, and is corrected here.

Reproduces exactly (gates 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7)

Recomputing from raw solves gives, to the digit: Spearman c16s2u 0.996, c24s4c 0.998; gate-6 trim (strict / trimmable) c16s2u 0.817° / 0.501°, c24s4c 0.692° / 0.442°, 7 untrimmable designs each. The ranking and decision machinery is sound and honestly reported.

Corrected: gate 4 was scored from a model, not the data

The original code set gate4 = stage5_eps < 1%, where stage5_eps is the Stage-5 planning model — worst-key error interpolated from Stage 4's four geometries at +4°, then span-corrected. But §7 + §4.6 require gate 4 to be the numerical uncertainty aggregated worst-case over geometry × angle, and Stage 6 had already solved every setting on all 30 designs. Measured directly from those solves (finest-grid discrepancy vs the c48s2c comparator, the finest mesh actually computed):

Gate 4 — modeled vs directly measured [worst-case %]
Settingmodel (orig)measured @+4°measured all αgate 4
c8s2u4.106.9636.15fail
c12s2u2.033.1915.26fail
c16s2u1.112.227.57fail
c24s4c0.792.955.21fail

The model was ~3× optimistic. Corrected, no setting clears gate 4 — including the production mesh, which the original report described as the unique gate-4 passer. The worst cells sit at α 0 with deflected elevons, where a coarse chordwise lattice resolves camber-driven loading least well; even at the clean +4° operating point every mesh is 2–7% out. This does not weaken the study's conclusion — it removes the "production is an adequate absolute-fidelity floor" reading and reinforces the escalate verdict: <1% on absolute effectiveness is unreachable at any tested mesh. The recomputation script is stage6_gate4_fix.py; numbers in stage6_gate4_measured.json.

Two honest limits of the whole exercise

The reference is not ground truth. "Error" everywhere means error against the densest AVL mesh (c48s2c), not against CFD or wind-tunnel. That mesh is itself ~1.5% short on elevon power (Stage 2), so every number is a self-consistency bound and reads optimistic in absolute terms. Separability was proven only on chord 8–16; the chord-24/48 shortlist members are a low-risk extrapolation, justified by monotone convergence but not directly demonstrated.

Synthesis & decision

The study did what it was built to do: it refused to hand back a falsely-cheap mesh. The evidence separates cleanly into two layers.

  • Ranking is safe at any mesh. ρ ≥ 0.99, 0% regret, 0 label flips, top-10 held (bar the deliberately-too-cheap c8), and Stage 6b shows this does not depend on the control state. An optimiser ranking designs would reach the same shortlist at c12 as at c48.
  • Absolute accuracy is not safe at any affordable mesh. Measured directly, gate 4 fails everywhere — worst-case coefficient error is ~3% even at production and rises to 5–36% at α 0. Gate 6's trim constraint is on the line at c16 and failed below it. The comparator itself is ~1.5% optimistic, so the true shortfall is larger still.
Recommendation

Screening / ranking sweeps → c16s2u at 19 h. The 7.3× saving over production is real and the ranking is provably intact (ρ 0.996, 0% regret, 0 label flips, control-state-independent). Its trim shift sits on the 0.50° line — fine for ranking, documented as a limitation.
Any run feeding absolute trim / control-authority numbers downstream → there is no clean mesh. c24s4c is the least-bad, but measured directly it carries ~3% worst-case coefficient error and does not clear gate 4; treat its absolute numbers as ~1.5–3% optimistic.
If the requirement is genuinely <1% on absolute effectiveness → escalate the model: no affordable AVL mesh delivers it; a higher-fidelity hinge/control-surface treatment is the correct fix, per §7.

Notably, if fidelity is being paid for anyway, the incumbent production choice is inefficient: its span-4 over-resolves the cheap axis and its cosine spacing is the worst performer (Stage 4). A chord-24/span-2/uniform mesh would very likely match c24s4c's accuracy at roughly half the cost — a follow-up worth one confirmatory run.

Appendix

Methods glossary

GCI
Grid Convergence Index — a Richardson-extrapolation error band with a safety factor (Fs = 1.25 here). Reported only where a quantity is monotone and in its asymptotic range.
observed order p
The convergence rate fitted from three meshes in ratio-2 refinement. p ≈ 1 means first-order; values out of range signal non-asymptotic behaviour.
finest-grid discrepancy
The honest fallback when Richardson is not licensed: the plain difference from the finest mesh actually computed. Bounds nothing for non-monotonic convergence — and says so.
interaction index I
rms(AB) / (rms(A)+rms(B)) from a two-way no-replication ANOVA. Small I ⇒ chordwise and spanwise are separable.
Spearman ρ
Rank correlation of designs by l_over_d against the comparator. ≥ 0.98 required, with a max-displacement clause.
objective regret
How much worse the design a cheap mesh would pick performs, judged by the reference — 0% means it picks the same winner.
delta_trim
−cm / elevon_sym.Cm — the elevon deflection to trim, per design per angle. Gate 6 caps its shift at 0.5°.
noise floor (§4.5)
1e−4. Below it, AVL's 6-digit print resolution makes relative error meaningless; the quantity is assessed on normalised discrepancy.
ε (worst key-quantity)
Worst-case error across the gate-4 quantities vs the dense-AVL comparator. "model ε" is the Stage-5 interpolated estimate; "measured ε" is the direct worst-case over all 30 designs — the correct gate-4 input (see §Validation).
comparator (c48s2c)
The densest AVL mesh actually run (chord 48, span 2). Used as the reference "truth" since no CFD is available — a self-consistency bound, itself ~1.5% short of reality on elevon power.

Reproducibility

Every solve is content-addressed by a provenance hash over the full pre-image: sample id, mesh (chord/span/spacing), α, β, both control inputs, viscous flag, velocity, altitude, the geometry-config SHA-256, the source git SHA, and the AVL binary version. Cache hits re-read and assert field-by-field equality; a mismatch is a hard stop. Scripts, locked config, summaries and these plots live under standalone/panelling_study/ and configs/aero/panelling_study/.

AVL Panelling Convergence Study · blended-wing-body · MACH-Aero / pyGeo / AVL · 1,165 runs across stages 0–7 · completed 2026-07-29.

Pre-registered gates, worst-case aggregation, honest error bounds. Result: escalate — no affordable mesh clears all seven gates; ranking is robust, control effectiveness is under-resolved.
